title: Fix it like a mechanic, not a guesser

beats.say: Your car makes a strange noise. Would you let a mechanic replace the engine without listening first?
A good mechanic hears the noise, lists likely causes, and tests each one. Only then do they touch a part. Debugging with an AI assistant works the same way.
The danger is that an AI is eager. It will confidently change code that was never broken. So you make it slow down: show me the bug, list suspects, prove which one, then fix.
Finally, you ask what else the fix might break. Five steps. Each one stops a confident guess from becoming a new bug.

check.q: Why make an AI assistant list causes and check them before changing code?
opts: It makes the AI answer faster
A confident guess may change code that was never the problem
It lets you skip writing tests
check.why: AI is eager and fluent, so a wrong theory sounds convincing. Checking causes first stops it editing healthy code.

work: Next time you hit a bug, write down the command that shows it before asking for help.
Add the words 'do not change code yet' to your first debugging prompt.

title: Reproduce, hypothesise, prove

beats.say: French revenue is a hundred times too high. What is the very first thing you ask the AI to do?

Reproduce it. Ask for one command, like running the pipeline for the first to the seventh of October, and print the totals. If you cannot make the bug appear on demand, you can never know you fixed it.
Next, hypothesise. Ask for three causes, most likely first, each with the quickest check. Say do not change code. Maybe a comma is being read as a decimal point.
Then prove. Show five French rows and what the parse function returns for each. Evidence beats explanation, because an AI can explain a wrong theory very fluently.

check.q: What should the hypothesise prompt include?
opts: Ranked causes, a quick check for each, and an instruction not to change code
A request to fix the most likely cause immediately
Only a description of the symptom
check.why: Ranked causes with cheap checks let you prove one cause, and the no-change rule keeps the AI from jumping to a fix.

work: Save your reproduction command in a notes file or a script.
Ask for the quickest confirming check for every suspected cause.
Use plan mode for the first three steps.

title: Test-first fix, then review

beats.say: How do you stop an AI fixing the wrong thing and calling it done?

Make it write a failing test first. Use one European amount, such as one thousand two hundred thirty-four and fifty cents, which should parse to 1234.50. Run it and watch it fail. That failure proves the test catches the bug.
Then ask for the smallest fix, and say do not change the test. Otherwise the AI may quietly edit the test until it passes.
Last, review. Ask what other inputs the fix could break and whether the same bug lives elsewhere. Read the diff yourself, and rerun the original command. The totals should now look right.

check.q: Why run the new test and see it fail before fixing?
opts: To warm up the test runner
To prove the test actually catches the bug
To make the fix shorter
check.why: A test that never failed might not test the bug at all. Seeing it fail, then pass, links the fix to the cause.

work: Insist on seeing the red test before accepting any fix.
After each fix, rerun the original reproduction command, not just the unit tests.

title: How green tests still lie

beats.say: Why can a green test still hide a broken fix?
Because the AI may write a test that only matches its own guess. Always see the test fail first, for the reason you expect. A test that never failed proves nothing.

Another trap is skipping the proof step. A plausible cause nobody checked often fixes the symptom, not the bug. Dividing French totals by one hundred makes the report look right while the parser stays wrong.

chip.text: Report looks right, data is wrong

beats.say: Also watch for edits that creep wide. A smallest fix touching ten files is a warning. Plan mode helps early on, because it can only read and run read-only checks.

check.q: The AI fixes French totals by dividing by 100 after parsing. What is wrong?
opts: Nothing, the report is correct now
It hides the symptom while the parser stays wrong
Division is always slow
check.why: The cause was never proven. The patch fixes one output and leaves the bad parsing to corrupt other values.

work: Reject any fix that you cannot trace back to a proven cause.
Check the diff size: a smallest fix should be small.
Look for tests edited in the same change as the fix.

title: When the loop is too much, or too little

beats.say: When is this five-step loop too much, and when is it not enough?

show.sub: to the cost of being wrong

beats.say: For a typo, the loop is overkill. A one-line fix with an obvious failing test needs only steps four and five. The cost of ceremony should match the cost of being wrong.
But money data, like revenue, deserves the full loop. A silent hundred-times error reaches dashboards and decisions before anyone notices.

Then scale it beyond one session. Keep the reproduction and the failing test in the repository, and run them in continuous integration so the bug cannot return. On risky systems, use plan mode for steps one to three.

check.q: Which change gives the best lasting protection after fixing a revenue parsing bug?
opts: Remember the bug for next time
Commit the regression test and run it in CI
Ask the AI to be more careful
check.why: An automated test turns one debugging session into permanent protection. Memory and good intentions do not.

work: Scale the loop to the blast radius: full loop for money and customer data.
Turn every proven bug into a committed regression test.
Require plan mode for the first three steps on production-critical pipelines.

title: The silenced smoke alarm

beats.say: Your smoke alarm beeps. You pull out the battery, and it goes quiet. Is the problem fixed?
No. The beep was only a symptom, a signal that something is wrong. You silenced the signal and never found the cause. Maybe it was a dying battery. Maybe it was smoke.
AI coding assistants can do the same. They see an error, recognise a familiar pattern, and name a likely cause. Often they are right. Sometimes they are confidently wrong.
And a wrong fix can quiet the symptom while the real bug stays hidden. So the rule is old and simple: no fix without evidence. Check first, then fix.

check.q: Why is it risky when an AI's fix makes an error disappear?
opts: The symptom may be hidden while the real cause remains
AI fixes always add new bugs
Errors that vanish are always intermittent
check.why: A vanished symptom does not show the cause was found. A wrong fix can mask the symptom and leave the bug in place, like pulling the battery from a smoke alarm.

work: Next time an AI proposes a fix, ask it: what evidence shows this is the cause?
Write down the symptom and the suspected cause as two separate sentences before accepting any change.

title: How a green check hides the bug

beats.say: Why would an AI fix a bug, turn the check green, and leave the bug in place?
Say report totals are off by a few cents. The model has seen this pattern often and says: rounding. It guesses from how the symptom looks, not from what the code actually did.
So it rounds the totals to whole dollars. The check passes. But the real fault is the parser, which cuts the cents off any value like 1,250.75. Every new row still loses money, now unseen.
Evidence breaks this. First reproduce the failure on a small input. Then prove the cause, for example by printing what the parser returns for one row. Only then fix, and rerun the same reproduction.

steps.label: Prove
steps.sub: print the parser output for one row

check.q: Totals are off by cents. An AI rounds the totals and the check passes. What is the best next step?
opts: Merge it, since the check is green
Reproduce on a small input and inspect what the parser returns for one row
Round to more decimal places
check.why: Rounding was a guess from the symptom. Inspecting actual parser output on a reproduction gives evidence of the real cause before any fix.

work: Ask the AI to give a failing reproduction before it proposes any change.
Print or log the intermediate value at the suspected step, and show it in the review.
Rerun the exact same reproduction after the fix and compare.

title: Fixes that only hide the symptom

beats.say: A fix made the error vanish. Why is that not proof you found the bug?
Because many wrong fixes hide symptoms. Wrap the call in a try block, add a retry, loosen the test, round the number. Each one silences the alarm and leaves the fault in place.

show.title: Fixes that mask
items: Swallow the error in a try block
Add a retry or a sleep

beats.say: Models also anchor. Once one says the cause is a timeout, later steps defend that story instead of testing it. And it only sees the code and logs you give it, so missing logs get filled with guesses.
Make the fix earn trust. The new test must fail before the change and pass after. Revert the fix and watch it fail again. Also confirm that the cause you named is the thing that actually changed.

check.q: An AI adds a test with its fix, and the test passes. What makes that test trustworthy evidence?
opts: It passes with the fix applied
It also fails when run against the code without the fix
It was written by the same model
check.why: A test that passes both with and without the fix proves nothing. It must fail on the old code and pass on the new, which ties the fix to the cause.

work: In reviews of AI fixes, run the new test against the base commit and confirm it fails.
Flag any fix that adds a try block, retry, sleep, or looser tolerance and ask what cause it addresses.
Give the AI complete logs and inputs, and tell it to say what it could not see.

title: Pricing the evidence rule

beats.say: Should every bug fix need proof? At scale, that rule has a price.
Proof costs time. For a one-line typo, or a compiler error that names the exact line, the error message is the evidence. Do not demand a ceremony there.
In a live incident, stop the bleeding first. Roll back or flip a flag. But call it mitigation, and keep the ticket open until the cause is proven.

steps.label: Mitigate
steps.sub: roll back or flip a flag

beats.say: To enforce it, build it into the pipeline. Require the pull request to state the cause, link the evidence, and include a test that fails on the old code. A separate reviewer, human or model, checks that chain. Rare race conditions need captured logs and traces, since you cannot reproduce them on demand.

show.title: Enforce in the pipeline
items: Test fails on the old code

check.q: A production outage is under way and the cause is unknown. What is the sound approach?
opts: Block all action until the root cause is proven
Mitigate with a rollback, label it as mitigation, then prove the cause afterward
Let the AI patch the most likely cause directly in production
check.why: Stopping harm quickly matters first, but a rollback is not a diagnosis. Labelling it mitigation and keeping the ticket open ensures the cause is still proven before it is called fixed.

work: Add a pull request template for bug fixes with cause, evidence, and a test that fails on the old code.
Define which bug classes get light checks and which need full proof, so effort follows risk.
Make sure rare, hard-to-reproduce failures have logs or traces captured in advance.

title: Why "it crashes" is not enough

beats.say: You call a mechanic and say, my car is broken. What can they do? Nothing, except guess.
Now say, it grinds when I brake, and it started after the tire change. Suddenly they know where to look. An AI agent is the same. It cannot see your screen. It only knows what you tell it.

chip.text: The agent can't see your screen

beats.say: So give four things. The exact error message. A tiny example that fails. What changed recently. And what you already checked, so it does not repeat your work.
Good evidence turns a guessing game into a short search.

show.sub: Say what you saw, not just that it broke

check.q: Why does an AI agent need you to describe the failure in detail?
opts: It only knows what you put in the conversation
It gets bored with short messages
Long messages make it run faster
check.why: The agent cannot see your screen or terminal. Exact errors, a small failing example and recent changes are its only clues, so vague input produces guesses.

work: Next time you report a bug, paste the full error text instead of describing it.
Add one line saying what you already tried.
Say when it last worked, if you know.

title: Five rows beat five gigabytes

beats.say: Which is better for debugging: a five gigabyte file, or five rows?
Five rows. The agent can read them at a glance, rerun the pipeline in seconds, and see which value breaks. A huge file takes minutes per try and hides the bad row.
Paste the exact command and the exact error, word for word. Then show what changed. Typing bang, git log, oneline, last ten, drops recent commits into the conversation. Or run git diff against main.
Finish with what you ruled out. If you already checked the schema, say so. Otherwise the agent spends its first attempt redoing your work.

check.q: A pipeline fails on a 5 GB file. What is the best evidence to give the agent?
opts: The whole file and the words "it crashes"
A few rows that still fail, plus the exact command and error
A summary of what you think the cause is
check.why: A small failing sample gives a fast rerun loop and exposes the bad value, while the exact command and error remove guessing.

work: Shrink every data bug to the fewest rows that still fail before asking for help.
Paste the command and error verbatim, never retyped.
Run git log in the chat so the agent sees recent changes.

title: Bisecting "it worked last week"

beats.say: It worked last week and now it fails. Which of two hundred commits broke it?

Git bisect answers by halving. It tests the middle commit, marks it good or bad, and repeats. Two hundred commits take about eight tests, not two hundred. Claude is very good at this mechanical search, if you give it a test command that exits zero on pass and nonzero on fail.

show.title: Tests needed to find the bad commit

beats.say: Now the gotchas. A flaky test sends bisect down the wrong half. A commit that will not build must be skipped. And the test must fail for the real reason, not a different error.

show.title: Where bisect goes wrong
items: Flaky test picks the wrong half
Test fails for a different reason
Bad commit may be a data change, not code

beats.say: So first run your test on a known good commit and a known bad one.

check.q: What does git bisect need from you to run automatically?
opts: A test command that passes or fails reliably
A list of suspect files
The author of the bad commit
check.why: Bisect halves the history using a pass or fail result. A reliable test command, with exit zero meaning pass, lets the agent run the search unattended.

work: Write a one-line test command that reproduces the bug before you start bisecting.
Run it on a known good and a known bad commit to confirm it fails for the right reason.
Rerun a flaky test several times, or fix it, before trusting bisect.

title: How much evidence is too much?

beats.say: Is more context always better evidence?

show.text: More context is not better evidence

beats.say: No. Dumping whole logs or a full dataset burns the context window, costs tokens, and buries the signal. A trimmed error with twenty lines around it beats ten thousand lines.
Also watch privacy. A five row sample from production may contain customer data. Mask it, or generate synthetic rows that still trigger the bug.

At team scale, make evidence a habit: a bug template with command, error, sample and recent changes, and a failing test in the repo. Bisect is the wrong tool when history is squashed or the bug lives in the data. Then diff the data instead.

show.title: Make it a team habit
items: Bug template: command, error, sample, changes
Failing test checked into the repo
Data-driven bug: diff the data, not the code

check.q: A bug appears only after a vendor changed an input file, and the code has not changed. What is the better move than git bisect?
opts: Bisect anyway with more commits
Compare the old and new input data to find what differs
Rewrite the pipeline
check.why: Bisect searches code history. If the code is unchanged, the cause is in the data, so diffing old and new inputs finds it directly.

work: Create a bug report template with command, error, small sample and recent changes.
Set a rule for masking or synthesizing production samples before sharing them with an agent.
Trim logs to the error plus a few lines of context before pasting.

title: The inspector before the storm

beats.say: Would you rather find a leak in your roof on a sunny day, or in the middle of a storm?

An AI agent can be a fixer, who patches things after they break. Or it can be an inspector, who walks the house and writes down what looks weak, ranked from worst to least. You tell it: review this file, rank problems by impact, and do not fix anything.
But an inspector can be wrong. A note saying the beam looks cracked is a lead, not a verdict. So ask for proof: show me the exact input that fails. Only then spend your afternoon on it.

show.title: Leads, not verdicts
items: Ask for the input that fails
Fix only what you can prove

check.q: An AI review says your loader has a serious bug. What is the best next step?
opts: Fix it immediately, since the AI is usually right
Ask for the exact input that triggers it and try it
Ignore it, because AI reviews are unreliable
check.why: Findings are leads. Asking for a failing input lets you confirm the issue cheaply before spending time on it, without trusting or dismissing it blindly.

work: Next time you open a risky file, ask for a ranked review with the words do not fix.
For every finding, write down the input that would prove it before you change code.

title: Four moves to catch bugs early

beats.say: How do you get an AI to find bugs that do not exist yet?

Move one: ask for a review of a single file through four lenses. Correctness, idempotency, which means safe to run twice, security, and performance. Ask for a ranking by impact, with file and line number, and say do not fix.
Move two: run the security review command on your pending changes. Move three: ask which code paths have no tests, and request the three tests most likely to catch a real bug.

show.title: Moves two and three
items: List code paths with no tests
Write the 3 most likely to catch a bug

beats.say: Move four: after any fix, search the repo for the same pattern. One bad date parse in one loader usually means a few more in the others. Bugs come in families.

check.q: Why ask the agent to search the repo for the same pattern after a fix?
opts: Bugs often repeat in sibling code written the same way
It makes the original fix run faster
It replaces the need for tests
check.why: The same mistake tends to be copied across similar files, so one fix often leaves siblings still broken.

work: Write a reusable review prompt with the four lenses and a ranking by impact with file:line.
After your next bug fix, run a repo-wide search for the same pattern before closing the ticket.
Ask for the three highest-value missing tests on your most critical pipeline.

title: When the reviewer is wrong

beats.say: Your AI reviewer just reported twelve issues. How many are real?
Maybe five. A reviewer reads code and guesses. It can invent problems, miss ones that depend on real data, and sound equally confident either way. So treat every finding as a lead.
Demand the failing input. If it claims the load duplicates rows on retry, ask for the exact file that causes it. Then run the load twice and count the rows. If you cannot reproduce it, drop it.
Also beware generated tests that only repeat what the code does. A test that passes on buggy code proves nothing. Break the code on purpose and check that the test fails.

show.title: Test the tests
items: Generated tests can mirror the bug
A good test must fail then

check.q: The agent writes a test that passes on your current code. What does that tell you about its value?
opts: It is valuable, because it passes
Little until you show it fails when the code is broken
It proves the code is correct
check.why: A test that cannot fail guards nothing. Mutating the code and seeing it fail shows the test actually checks behavior.

work: For each reported issue, get a failing input or a repro script before you touch code.
Run the load twice on the same data and compare row counts to test idempotency yourself.
Mutate the code once to confirm each new AI-written test fails.

title: Where AI review earns its cost

beats.say: Should an AI review replace your linters, tests and human reviewers?

No. It is a probabilistic extra layer. Linters and type checks are cheap, deterministic and run on every commit. AI review costs tokens, varies from run to run, and on a big repo you must aim it at risky code like loaders, money movement and permissions.
Use it where rules cannot reach: logic errors, idempotency and missing tests. Run it on the diff before merge, not on the whole repo every day.
Then make findings permanent. When it exposes a bug family, encode it as a lint rule or a CI test. The check becomes free, and no longer depends on a model.

check.q: An AI review reveals a family of unsafe date parses across your loaders. What is the best long-term response?
opts: Re-run the AI review monthly
Add a lint rule or CI test that catches the pattern
Trust the team to remember it
check.why: Encoding the pattern as a deterministic check makes detection free and consistent, and removes dependence on a variable, costly model.

work: Target AI review at the diff of high-risk code instead of the whole repo.
Keep linters, types and CI as the base layer, and treat AI review as extra.
Convert each confirmed bug family into a lint rule or regression test.
